questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman has a routine plasma sodium of 128 mEq/L. She is asymptomatic. The clinician categorizes her hyponatremia by severity. Which of the following correctly classifies her hyponatremia and the typical severity bands?
choices: Moderate hyponatremia (Na+ 125–129) — patients are often asymptomatic or have mild symptoms (nausea, mild confusion); 'mild' typically refers to 130–134; 'severe' to <125 (often symptomatic with confusion, seizures, herniation if acute). The same Na+ value can be benign (chronic) or life-threatening (acute) depending on rate of development
explanations: Incorrect. Severe hyponatremia is typically defined as Na+ <125 mEq/L; this patient is at 128.

Correct. The classical severity classification of hyponatremia: MILD = Na+ 130–134; MODERATE = Na+ 125–129; SEVERE = Na+ <125. This patient at 128 is in the MODERATE range. Symptoms depend on both the absolute Na+ and the rate of development: chronic hyponatremia at any given Na+ level is far less symptomatic than acute hyponatremia (because brain idiogenic osmole adaptation defends brain volume). A patient with chronic Na+ 110 may be lucid, while an athlete with acute Na+ 125 may seize. Severity classification guides URGENCY of treatment but symptom severity guides INTENSITY: severely symptomatic hyponatremia (regardless of absolute value) requires hypertonic saline; chronic asymptomatic hyponatremia is approached more cautiously.
Incorrect. 130–134 is mild; this patient is at 128.
Incorrect. The Na+ here is 128, not 134; and asymptomatic is a clinical category.
Incorrect. Pseudohyponatremia is a specific etiology (lab artifact from hyperlipidemia/hyperproteinemia); not described here.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old marathon runner collapses at mile 22 with seizure. Plasma sodium is 121 mEq/L. He had been hyponatremic for less than 4 hours. A 65-year-old woman with chronic SIADH from small cell lung cancer has had plasma sodium 121 for 2 weeks; she is alert and oriented. Which of the following best explains why the marathon runner has dramatic symptoms while the elderly patient does not, despite identical sodium levels?
choices: The marathon runner has additional cerebral injury

Acute (<48 hours) vs chronic (>48 hours) hyponatremia produce dramatically different clinical pictures at the same plasma Na+. ACUTE hyponatremia: brain cells have not had time to adapt by losing idiogenic osmoles, so water shifts into brain cells producing CEREBRAL EDEMA → confusion, seizure, coma, herniation. CHRONIC hyponatremia: brain cells defend their volume by extruding idiogenic osmoles (myo-inositol, taurine, glutamine) within 24–48 hours, reducing intracellular osmolality to match ECF; symptoms are usually mild despite the same Na+. CRITICAL CONSEQUENCE: the same Na+ correction rate that is safe in acute hyponatremia (rapid correction, no ODS risk because cells haven't lost osmoles) can produce ODS in chronic hyponatremia (rapid water shift OUT of brain cells before osmoles can be replenished)
Sodium has different effects in different age groups
Plasma sodium does not correlate with symptoms
explanations: Incorrect. The marathon runner's symptoms are from cerebral edema due to acute hyponatremia, not additional injury.
Incorrect. Chronic SIADH commonly produces minimal symptoms at low Na+; not a misdiagnosis.

Correct. The acute vs chronic distinction is THE central concept in clinical hyponatremia. ACUTE hyponatremia (developing within hours) produces dramatic symptoms (cerebral edema, seizures, herniation) because brain cells have not yet adapted to defend their volume. CHRONIC hyponatremia (developing over days to weeks) is far better tolerated because brain cells extrude idiogenic osmoles (organic osmolytes — myo-inositol, glutamine, taurine, glutamate) over 24–48 hours, reducing intracellular osmolality to match ECF and preventing brain edema. The CRITICAL therapeutic implication: acute hyponatremia can be corrected RAPIDLY with hypertonic saline (no ODS risk because brain hasn't lost osmoles); chronic hyponatremia must be corrected SLOWLY (≤8 mEq/L/24h) because rapid restoration of plasma Na+ shifts water OUT of brain cells before osmoles can be rebuilt — producing osmotic demyelination syndrome.
Incorrect. The pathophysiology is identical; the difference is duration of hyponatremia.
Incorrect. Plasma Na+ does correlate with symptoms when adjusted for duration.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman is found to have plasma sodium 122 mEq/L on routine labs. Her clinician follows the diagnostic algorithm shown in the diagram below. After confirming a low plasma sodium, what is the appropriate NEXT step in the workup?
questions.diagram:
Diagnostic algorithm for hyponatremia
1. Confirm low plasma Na+ (rule out lab error)
2. Measure plasma osmolality
→ HIGH (mannitol, hyperglycemia): translational hyponatremia
→ NORMAL (lipids, proteins): pseudohyponatremia (lab artifact)
→ LOW: TRUE hypotonic hyponatremia → assess volume status
3. Hypovolemic / Euvolemic / Hypervolemic determine etiology
4. Urine osmolality + urine sodium to refine
choices: Measure plasma osmolality to determine whether the hyponatremia is hypotonic (true), isotonic (pseudohyponatremia), or hypertonic (translational/hyperosmolar). This first branch of the algorithm distinguishes lab artifact (lipids, proteins) and translational shifts (hyperglycemia, mannitol) from TRUE hypotonic hyponatremia, which requires further volume assessment
explanations: Incorrect. Treatment is initiated only after etiology and severity are determined.

Correct. The first branch of the hyponatremia algorithm uses plasma osmolality to distinguish three categories: (1) HYPOTONIC (true) hyponatremia — Posm <275; the most common form; reflects free water excess relative to sodium. Requires volume assessment for further classification. (2) ISOTONIC (pseudohyponatremia) — Posm normal (~280–295); caused by severe hyperlipidemia or hyperproteinemia displacing water in plasma sample. The Na+ measurement is artifactually low; actual sodium homeostasis is intact. (3) HYPERTONIC (translational) — Posm >295; caused by accumulation of effective osmoles (glucose in DKA/HHS; mannitol therapy) drawing water out of cells, diluting plasma Na+. Total body Na+ is unchanged; the hyponatremia is appropriate for the elevated osmolality. Each category has different management — pseudohyponatremia needs no treatment; translational corrects with treatment of the underlying osmole; true hypotonic requires further workup.
Incorrect. Free water restriction is one possible treatment but only after etiology is established.
Incorrect. MRI is only relevant for select etiologies (e.g., suspected central DI or pituitary mass), not the general initial step.
Incorrect. Dialysis is reserved for severe/refractory cases.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma has plasma sodium 128 mEq/L on routine labs. Plasma osmolality (measured directly by osmometer) is 285 mOsm/kg — within the normal range. Other laboratory studies are shown.
choices: Pseudohyponatremia from massive paraprotein elevation in multiple myeloma — paraproteins displace water in the plasma volume, falsely lowering Na+ measurement when sodium is reported as mEq per total plasma volume (some flame photometry methods). The MEASURED plasma osmolality is NORMAL (since sodium homeostasis is actually intact), but the calculated osmolality is artifactually low because it uses the artifactually low Na+. Direct ion-selective electrode methods on undiluted samples are not affected by this artifact. NO TREATMENT for the 'hyponatremia' is needed — the patient's actual sodium homeostasis is normal
Hypovolemic hyponatremia from extra-renal Na+ losses
explanations: Correct. Pseudohyponatremia is a LABORATORY ARTIFACT, not a true sodium disorder. Mechanism: in normal plasma, sodium is dissolved in the aqueous fraction (~93% of plasma volume). When sodium is reported as 'mEq per liter of plasma,' the calculation assumes the normal aqueous fraction. In severe hyperlipidemia or hyperproteinemia (multiple myeloma, Waldenstrom), the lipid/protein component of plasma expands, REDUCING the aqueous fraction. The actual Na+ concentration in the AQUEOUS phase is normal, but the reported Na+ (per total plasma volume) is artifactually low. Old flame photometry methods are particularly susceptible; direct potentiometric (ion-selective electrode) measurement on undiluted plasma is not affected. KEY DIAGNOSTIC FEATURE: measured plasma osmolality is NORMAL (because sodium homeostasis is actually intact); calculated osmolality (using the false low Na+) is artifactually low. No 'osmolar gap' exists in pseudohyponatremia in the usual sense. NO TREATMENT is needed for the hyponatremia — the sodium is actually normal. Recognition prevents inappropriate therapy.
Incorrect. SIADH features LOW measured plasma osmolality and inappropriately concentrated urine; this patient has NORMAL measured Posm.
Incorrect. Translational hyponatremia features HIGH measured plasma osmolality (from glucose/mannitol); this patient has normal Posm.
Incorrect. CSW features hypovolemia and HIGH urine Na+; not described here.
Incorrect. Hypovolemic hyponatremia would feature signs of volume depletion and low urine Na+.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes is admitted in DKA. Her plasma glucose is 580 mg/dL and plasma sodium is 131 mEq/L. Her clinician notes that the plasma sodium is below normal range. Which of the following best characterizes the mechanism and corrected sodium in this patient?
choices: Pseudohyponatremia from elevated lipids in DKA

Translational (hyperosmolar) hyponatremia from hyperglycemia: glucose is an EFFECTIVE osmole in the low-insulin state of DKA (cellular glucose uptake is impaired); the elevated plasma glucose draws water OUT of cells INTO plasma by osmosis, diluting plasma sodium WITHOUT changing total body sodium. The CORRECTED sodium = measured Na+ + 1.6 × (glucose − 100)/100 = 131 + 1.6 × (580−100)/100 = 131 + 7.7 ≈ 139 (normal). With insulin therapy, glucose falls and water shifts back into cells, allowing Na+ to normalize. The 'hyponatremia' is benign and protective; no Na+ replacement is needed
explanations: Incorrect. DKA does not feature severe hyperlipidemia; the mechanism is osmotic translation, not lab artifact.
Incorrect. SIADH features low plasma osmolality with concentrated urine; DKA features HIGH plasma osmolality from glucose.
Incorrect. CSW occurs in CNS disease, not DKA.
Incorrect. Hypovolemia from osmotic diuresis is real in DKA, but the dominant mechanism for the hyponatremia per se is the osmotic translation by hyperglycemia.

Correct. Hyperglycemia produces translational hyponatremia by drawing water OUT of cells into ECF (glucose is an effective osmole when insulin is deficient). For every 100 mg/dL glucose above 100 mg/dL, plasma sodium is depressed by approximately 1.6 mEq/L. CORRECTED Na+ = measured + 1.6 × (glucose − 100)/100. For glucose 580 and Na+ 131: corrected = 131 + 1.6 × 4.8 = 131 + 7.7 ≈ 139 (within normal range). With insulin therapy, glucose falls, water shifts back into cells, and plasma Na+ rises. The 'hyponatremia' is benign and even protective (defending brain volume against the hyperosmolar plasma); no Na+ replacement is needed. Understanding this prevents inappropriate Na+ administration in DKA, which could contribute to cerebral edema during glucose correction.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man with newly diagnosed small cell lung cancer presents with euvolemic hyponatremia. Plasma sodium 122, plasma osmolality 252, urine osmolality 580, urine sodium 80. He has no thyroid or adrenal abnormality. Which of the following best characterizes the diagnostic features of SIADH in this patient?
choices: Hypotonic euvolemic hyponatremia with INAPPROPRIATELY CONCENTRATED urine (Uosm >100 mOsm/kg, usually >300), urine sodium >40 mEq/L (kidney handles Na+ normally), euvolemic clinical exam, and exclusion of thyroid/adrenal/renal causes. The mechanism is inappropriately elevated ADH (often from paraneoplastic ectopic secretion in SCLC) that drives water reabsorption in the collecting duct despite low plasma osmolality. Treatment: free water restriction; tolvaptan for chronic management; hypertonic saline for severely symptomatic
explanations: Incorrect. SIADH features EUVOLEMIA (not hypervolemia); ADH is elevated.

Correct. SIADH diagnostic criteria (Schwartz-Bartter): (1) plasma osmolality <275 mOsm/kg (this patient: 252); (2) inappropriately concentrated urine (Uosm >100 mOsm/kg; this patient: 580); (3) urine sodium ≥40 mEq/L on normal sodium intake (this patient: 80, reflecting normal renal Na+ handling); (4) clinical euvolemia (no orthostatic changes, no edema); (5) exclusion of thyroid, adrenal, renal causes; (6) no recent diuretic use. The patient meets all criteria for SIADH. SCLC accounts for ~70% of paraneoplastic SIADH (ectopic ADH secretion by tumor cells). Treatment: (a) free water restriction (≤800 mL/day) — first-line; (b) hypertonic saline for severely symptomatic; (c) tolvaptan (V2 antagonist) for chronic management refractory to restriction; (d) treat underlying disease.
Incorrect. SIADH is EUVOLEMIC, not hypovolemic.
Incorrect. Pseudohyponatremia features NORMAL plasma osmolality (lab artifact); this patient has clearly low Posm (252).
Incorrect. Translational hyponatremia features HIGH plasma osmolality from glucose; this patient's Posm is low.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man presents with 3 days of vomiting and watery diarrhea, dry mucous membranes, and orthostatic hypotension. He has continued to drink water but no electrolytes. Laboratory studies are shown.
choices: Hypovolemic hypotonic hyponatremia from extra-renal Na+ + water loss with disproportionate plain-water replacement: GI losses (vomiting/diarrhea) remove Na+ AND water but he replaces with plain water; the extra water relative to Na+ dilutes plasma sodium. The kidney's RESPONSE is appropriate — RAAS, SNS, and ADH activation produce avid Na+ retention (UNa <20, low FENa) and water retention (concentrated urine, high BUN:Cr). Treatment is isotonic saline to replace both Na+ and ECF volume; plasma Na+ corrects as Na+ losses are repaired and the volume stimulus to ADH is removed
explanations: Incorrect. SIADH features EUVOLEMIA with HIGH urine Na+ (>40); this patient is hypovolemic with LOW urine Na+.
Incorrect. CSW features hypovolemia AND HIGH urine Na+ (>40 from inappropriate renal Na+ wasting); this patient has appropriately LOW urine Na+ (12) reflecting renal Na+ avidity.

Correct. Hypovolemic hypotonic hyponatremia from extra-renal Na+ + water loss with disproportionate water replacement is one of the most common scenarios. Mechanism: GI losses remove gastric/intestinal fluid (Na+ ~120–130 mEq/L, slightly hypotonic to plasma); the patient drinks plain water without electrolytes; over time, more water than Na+ is replaced, lowering plasma Na+. Concurrent volume contraction activates RAAS (high renin and aldo), SNS, and ADH (volume stimulus overrides osmotic suppression). The kidney's response is APPROPRIATE: avid Na+ retention (UNa <20, low FENa <1%, BUN:Cr >20) and water retention (concentrated urine, Uosm 510). The urine indices distinguish from SIADH (where UNa is >40 and patient is euvolemic). Treatment: isotonic saline to replace BOTH the volume and Na+ deficit; plasma Na+ rises as the volume stimulus to ADH is removed.
Incorrect. Pseudohyponatremia features NORMAL Posm; this patient's Posm is clearly low.
Incorrect. HF would present with HYPERVOLEMIA (edema, JVD), not the dry membranes and orthostatic hypotension of this patient.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man with end-stage HFrEF has gained 10 kg of fluid weight, has elevated jugular venous pressure, peripheral edema, and ascites. Plasma sodium is 124 mEq/L, plasma osmolality 252, urine sodium 8, urine osmolality 480. Which of the following best characterizes his hyponatremia?
choices: HYPERVOLEMIC hyponatremia from heart failure: total body water and Na+ are markedly INCREASED, but EAV is reduced (low cardiac output / arterial underfilling). The kidney 'sees' the patient as volume-depleted and activates RAAS, SNS, and ADH. Free water retention is disproportionate to Na+ retention (because non-osmotic ADH release favors water over salt), so plasma Na+ falls despite total body Na+ excess. Urine Na+ is LOW (<20) because RAAS-driven Na+ retention dominates. Treatment: loop diuretic for volume, free water restriction; tolvaptan for severe symptomatic hyponatremia; treat underlying HF
explanations: Incorrect. SIADH features EUVOLEMIA; this patient has overt volume overload (edema, JVD, weight gain).
Incorrect. The patient has volume overload, not depletion.
Incorrect. Pseudohyponatremia features NORMAL plasma osmolality; this patient has clearly low Posm.

Correct. HF illustrates the central paradox of EAV physiology: total body Na+ and water are markedly INCREASED (manifested as edema, ascites, weight gain), but EFFECTIVE arterial volume is REDUCED (low cardiac output → arterial underfilling). The kidney senses arterial underfilling at baroreceptors, JG cells, and macula densa, and activates RAAS, SNS, and (especially) non-osmotic ADH. Free water retention is disproportionate to Na+ retention because the ADH stimulus is severe — overriding the osmotic suppression that would normally occur with low Posm. Plasma Na+ falls despite total body Na+ excess (dilutional/hypervolemic hyponatremia). Urine Na+ is LOW (<20) because RAAS-driven Na+ retention dominates. TREATMENT: loop diuretic for volume; free water restriction (1.0–1.5 L/day); tolvaptan for severe symptomatic hyponatremia; treat underlying HF (RAAS blockade, β-blocker, ARNi, SGLT2i). Severe hyponatremia in HF carries strong prognostic significance.
Incorrect. Translational hyponatremia features HIGH plasma osmolality from glucose/mannitol; this patient's Posm is low.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with chronic alcohol use disorder and minimal solid food intake (subsisting mostly on beer for the past 3 weeks) presents with confusion. Plasma sodium is 119 mEq/L, plasma osmolality 248, urine sodium 25, urine osmolality 105 (DILUTE). Volume status is mildly hypovolemic. Which of the following best characterizes his hyponatremia?
choices: Beer potomania — chronic excessive beer intake (high water content, low solute) combined with minimal solute intake from food. The kidney's diluting capacity is normally limited by the solute load delivered to the diluting segments; with intake of only ~250–500 mOsm/day of solute (vs normal ~600–900), maximum free water excretion may be only 4–5 L (rather than the usual 18–20 L). Even modest beer intake (8–10 L/day) overwhelms this reduced capacity, producing dilutional hyponatremia. Urine osmolality is LOW (~50–100) reflecting maximal ADH suppression — distinguishing from SIADH. Treatment: thiamine (avoid Wernicke), gradual rehydration with isotonic saline + dietary solute; CAUTION with rapid correction because of high ODS risk in chronic hyponatremia + alcoholism + malnutrition
explanations: Incorrect. SIADH features CONCENTRATED urine; this patient has DILUTE urine (ADH appropriately suppressed).
Incorrect. CSW occurs in CNS disease and features HIGH urine Na+ (>40); this patient has low UNa and no CNS pathology.
Incorrect. Translational hyponatremia features HIGH Posm; this patient's Posm is low.
Incorrect. Cirrhotic hyponatremia features hypervolemia (ascites, edema) with concentrated urine; this patient has dilute urine.

Correct. Beer potomania (and the related 'tea-and-toast hyponatremia' in elderly patients with poor solute intake) results from solute intake too low to permit adequate free water excretion. The kidney's free water excretion is limited by the solute load: water excretion (in L/day) ≈ solute excretion / minimum urine osmolality. With intake of 250–500 mOsm/day of solute (vs normal 600–900), and minimum urine osmolality of 50 mOsm/kg, maximum water excretion is only 5–10 L/day. Modest beer intake (8–10 L/day) easily overwhelms this. ADH is appropriately suppressed (urine osm low, ~50–150). Distinguishes from SIADH by the DILUTE urine. RISK: very high for ODS during correction because of the combination of chronic hyponatremia + alcoholism + malnutrition + hypokalemia. Treatment must be SLOW (≤6 mEq/L/24h), include thiamine to prevent Wernicke, and gradual rehydration with isotonic saline plus dietary solute. Many patients self-correct simply with re-feeding if water intake is limited.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old widowed woman who lives alone, eats very little, and drinks several cups of tea daily presents with confusion. Plasma sodium 120, plasma osmolality 248, urine sodium 18, urine osmolality 80 (DILUTE). Volume status is borderline. Which of the following best characterizes her hyponatremia?
choices: 'Tea-and-toast' hyponatremia — analogous to beer potomania but driven by inadequate dietary solute intake (low protein, low salt). Solute excretion is too low to permit adequate free water excretion (low solute load + minimal urine osm = limited free water excretion). Even modest fluid intake exceeds excretory capacity, producing dilutional hyponatremia. Urine osm is LOW (ADH appropriately suppressed). Common in elderly, malnourished, or socially isolated patients on minimal-solute diets. Treatment: gradual rehydration plus dietary solute; CAUTION with rapid correction because of ODS risk in chronic + malnourished
explanations: Correct. 'Tea-and-toast' hyponatremia is the elderly equivalent of beer potomania. The mechanism: very low dietary solute intake (minimal protein, low salt — typical of social isolation, depression, or financial limitation) reduces daily solute excretion to only 200–400 mOsm/day. The kidney's free water excretion is solute-limited: max water excretion (L) ≈ solute excretion / minimum Uosm. With low solute and minimum Uosm of 50–80, maximum water excretion may be only 3–4 L/day. Even modest fluid intake (tea, soup, water) exceeds this capacity, producing dilutional hyponatremia. Urine osmolality is LOW (~50–150) reflecting MAXIMAL ADH suppression — distinguishing from SIADH (where Uosm is high). Common in elderly malnourished or socially isolated patients. Risk for ODS during correction is HIGH (chronic + malnutrition + often hypokalemia). Treatment: gradual rehydration (correction limit ≤6 mEq/L/24h), dietary solute supplementation, address social/nutrition issues. Often patients self-correct with re-feeding.
Incorrect. SIADH features CONCENTRATED urine; this patient has dilute urine.
Incorrect. CSW occurs in CNS disease.
Incorrect. HF features hypervolemia and concentrated urine.
Incorrect. Pseudohyponatremia features NORMAL Posm; this patient's Posm is low.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old recreational marathon runner collapses at mile 22 with seizure. He had been drinking water at every aid station and 'overhydrating' to prevent dehydration. Plasma sodium 120 mEq/L, plasma osmolality 252, urine osmolality 480. Which of the following best characterizes his hyponatremia?
choices: Exercise-associated hyponatremia (EAH): excessive water intake during prolonged exertion, often combined with non-osmotic ADH release driven by exertion-related stress, NSAID use, and elevated cytokines, overwhelms renal free water excretion and produces dilutional hyponatremia. Risk factors: prolonged events (marathons, ultramarathons, triathlons), excessive water/sports-drink intake, female sex, longer race times, NSAIDs, hot weather. The hyponatremia is ACUTE (developed during the race, <hours), so cerebral edema risk is HIGH and dramatic symptoms (seizure, coma) may occur. Treatment: hypertonic 3% saline IV bolus; FREE WATER RESTRICTION; correct rapidly because acute hyponatremia (no ODS risk in acute setting). Prevention: drink to thirst rather than scheduled volumes
explanations: Incorrect. The mechanism is excessive water intake (overhydration), not dehydration; though both contribute to runner electrolyte issues.

Correct. Exercise-associated hyponatremia (EAH) is increasingly recognized in endurance athletes. Mechanism: (1) excessive water/sports-drink intake during prolonged exertion (often more than the ~750–1000 mL/h that the kidney can excrete); (2) non-osmotic ADH release driven by exertion-related stress, NSAID use (impair water excretion), elevated cytokines, and SIADH-like syndromes; (3) some patients have unrecognized SIADH-prone physiology. Risk factors: long events (marathons, ultramarathons, triathlons), excessive water intake, female sex (slower race times → more time to drink), NSAID use, hot weather. EAH is ACUTE (develops over hours), so brain has not adapted — cerebral edema risk is HIGH and dramatic symptoms (seizure, coma) may occur even at modest absolute Na+ values. Treatment: hypertonic 3% saline IV (e.g., 100 mL boluses) for symptomatic; free water restriction; isotonic saline can WORSEN hyponatremia in acute SIADH-like physiology so 3% is preferred. Because acute hyponatremia carries low ODS risk, rapid correction is acceptable and even preferred. Prevention: 'drink to thirst' rather than scheduled volumes; sports drinks alone do not prevent EAH (Na+ content is too low).
Incorrect. Rhabdomyolysis would feature elevated CK and possibly hyperkalemia, not hyponatremia from this mechanism.
Incorrect. Sports drinks contain glucose but at concentrations far below hyperosmolar levels.
Incorrect. Chronic SIADH would have a different temporal pattern (not acute development during race).

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman on hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension is admitted with confusion and plasma sodium 118 mEq/L. She has been on HCTZ for 3 weeks and increased her water intake recently. Which of the following best characterizes thiazide-induced hyponatremia?
choices: Multifactorial: thiazide blockade of NCC impairs the diluting segment in the DCT; volume contraction triggers non-osmotic ADH release; concurrent hypokalemia (very common with chronic thiazide) impairs renal water handling; increased water intake (from thirst, dry mouth) overwhelms reduced excretory capacity; elderly patients are particularly susceptible due to age-related impairment of renal water handling. Often associated with mild volume depletion. Management: stop thiazide; correct hyponatremia cautiously (≤8 mEq/L/24h); replace K+; switch to alternative antihypertensive (CCB, ACEi, ARB, loop diuretic — which causes hyponatremia much less often)
Cerebral salt wasting from drug effect
explanations: Incorrect. Thiazide-induced hyponatremia is typically associated with HYPOkalemia (not hyperkalemia).

Correct. Thiazide-induced hyponatremia is multifactorial: (1) NCC blockade in the early DCT impairs urinary dilution (the DCT is part of the diluting segment); (2) volume contraction triggers non-osmotic ADH release, enhancing water reabsorption at the collecting duct (free water retention disproportionate to Na+ retention); (3) concurrent hypokalemia from the thiazide impairs ADH suppression and renal water handling; (4) increased water intake from thirst overwhelms reduced excretory capacity; (5) elderly patients particularly susceptible due to age-related impairment of renal water handling. Often associated with mild volume depletion (not the typical 'euvolemic SIADH' picture). Management: STOP THIAZIDE; correct hyponatremia cautiously (≤8 mEq/L/24h); replete K+ (often refractory hypokalemia from concurrent hypomagnesemia); switch to alternative antihypertensive (CCB, ACEi, ARB, or even loop diuretic — which causes hyponatremia much less often than thiazides).
Incorrect. Thiazide does not cause translational hyponatremia.
Incorrect. Thiazide does not cause pseudohyponatremia.
Incorrect. CSW occurs in CNS disease, not from thiazide.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old woman with major depressive disorder was started on sertraline 6 weeks ago and now presents with confusion and weakness. Laboratory studies are shown.
choices: SSRI (sertraline)-induced SIADH — SSRIs are a recognized cause of SIADH, particularly in elderly women within the first weeks of therapy. Mechanism is thought to involve enhanced ADH release. The pattern matches euvolemic hypotonic hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine and elevated UNa — classic for SIADH. Other drugs causing SIADH include carbamazepine, vincristine, chemotherapeutics (cyclophosphamide), and MDMA. Management: stop SSRI; consider switching to bupropion (doesn't cause SIADH); free water restriction; tolvaptan if severe; hypertonic saline for severely symptomatic with seizure
explanations: Incorrect. HF features hypervolemia (edema, JVD); this patient is euvolemic.
Incorrect. Hypovolemic hyponatremia features dry mucous membranes, orthostatic hypotension, and LOW urine Na+; this patient has high UNa and is euvolemic.
Incorrect. Pseudohyponatremia features NORMAL plasma osmolality.

Correct. SSRIs (especially sertraline, fluoxetine, paroxetine) are a well-recognized cause of SIADH, particularly in elderly women within the first weeks of therapy. The pattern matches all SIADH criteria: (1) plasma osmolality <275 (248); (2) inappropriately concentrated urine (Uosm 510); (3) urine Na+ >40 (65); (4) euvolemic; (5) excluded thyroid/adrenal causes. Mechanism is thought to involve serotonin-mediated enhancement of ADH release at the hypothalamus. Management: stop the SSRI; bupropion (which doesn't cause SIADH) is a reasonable alternative for depression; free water restriction; tolvaptan for chronic management; hypertonic 3% saline for severely symptomatic with seizure or coma. Other drugs causing SIADH include carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, MDMA (ecstasy), and many others. Recognition is important because the offending drug needs to be stopped or switched.
Incorrect. Translational hyponatremia features HIGH plasma osmolality from glucose/mannitol.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman with primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) presents with hyponatremia of 124 mEq/L, hyperkalemia (K+ 5.8), and orthostatic hypotension. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of hyponatremia in this patient?
choices: Combined glucocorticoid AND mineralocorticoid deficiency: (1) aldosterone deficiency produces renal Na+ wasting (hypovolemia + low UNa surprisingly) and K+ retention (hyperkalemia, mild metabolic acidosis); (2) cortisol deficiency removes its normal tonic inhibition of ADH release, producing inappropriate ADH-driven free water retention; the volume depletion from aldosterone deficiency further drives non-osmotic ADH release. The combination of Na+ loss + free water retention produces hypovolemic hypotonic hyponatremia. Treatment: hydrocortisone (cortisol replacement) corrects the ADH-driven water retention rapidly; fludrocortisone (mineralocorticoid replacement) corrects the renal Na+ wasting. Recognition is critical — adrenal insufficiency can present primarily as hyponatremia
explanations: Incorrect. Pseudohyponatremia is a lab artifact unrelated to ACTH or adrenal disease.
Incorrect. Translational hyponatremia features HIGH plasma osmolality; not the case here.
Incorrect. Adrenal insufficiency features HYPOvolemia, not hypervolemia.
Incorrect. CSW occurs in CNS disease, not adrenal insufficiency.

Correct. Hyponatremia in adrenal insufficiency results from combined glucocorticoid AND mineralocorticoid deficiency. The mechanism: (1) aldosterone deficiency → renal Na+ wasting (this paradoxically can produce volume depletion with relatively LOW urine Na+ once volume status drops further); K+ retention (hyperkalemia); mild metabolic acidosis (impaired H+ secretion); (2) cortisol deficiency → loss of cortisol's normal tonic inhibition of CRH and ADH; inappropriate ADH-driven free water retention contributes to hyponatremia. Volume depletion further drives non-osmotic ADH release. The combination is hypovolemic hypotonic hyponatremia with hyperkalemia — a very characteristic pattern. Recognition is important because adrenal insufficiency can PRESENT as hyponatremia. Treatment: hydrocortisone (corrects the ADH-driven water retention and supports stress response); fludrocortisone (corrects renal Na+ wasting and hyperkalemia); IV saline. Hyponatremia from adrenal crisis can be life-threatening; cosyntropin stimulation testing diagnoses primary adrenal insufficiency.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman with severe untreated primary hypothyroidism (TSH 145, FT4 0.2) presents with hyponatremia of 122 mEq/L. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of hyponatremia in severe hypothyroidism?
choices: Severe hypothyroidism reduces cardiac output and GFR, lowering free water excretion capacity. The reduced GFR limits filtered water that can be excreted; ADH levels may also be inappropriately elevated. Coexisting reduced cellular metabolic activity may impair Na+/K+-ATPase function. The hyponatremia is typically mild-to-moderate and resolves with thyroid hormone replacement (slowly over weeks). Severe hypothyroidism can also unmask SIADH-like physiology. Recognition matters because thyroid hormone replacement, not water restriction alone, is the definitive treatment
explanations: Correct. Hyponatremia in severe hypothyroidism (myxedema) is multifactorial: (1) reduced cardiac output and GFR limit filtered water — the kidney cannot excrete water faster than it can filter it; (2) ADH levels may be inappropriately elevated, possibly mediated by reduced cardiac output and hemodynamic effects; (3) reduced cellular metabolic activity may impair Na+/K+-ATPase function and intracellular volume regulation; (4) severe hypothyroidism can unmask SIADH-like physiology in some patients. The hyponatremia is typically mild to moderate (Na+ 130–135) but can be severe in myxedema coma. Resolution is gradual with levothyroxine replacement, often over 1–4 weeks. Importantly, recognition prevents inappropriate water restriction alone — thyroid hormone replacement is the definitive treatment. In myxedema coma, IV levothyroxine and supportive care are needed; severe hyponatremia may require hypertonic saline.
Incorrect. TSH does not cause pseudohyponatremia.
Incorrect. Hypothyroidism does not cause hyperglycemia.
Incorrect. Severe hypothyroidism causes pericardial effusion but rarely hypervolemic hyponatremia from HF physiology.
Incorrect. CSW occurs in CNS disease.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman is hospitalized after hip arthroplasty. She receives 3 L of intravenous 0.45% saline and 5% dextrose in water (D5W) over 24 hours. On postoperative day 2 she develops confusion. Plasma sodium has fallen from 140 to 124 mEq/L. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of postoperative hyponatremia?
choices: Postoperative SIADH-like physiology (driven by surgical stress, pain, opioids, nausea — all promoting non-osmotic ADH release) PLUS administration of hypotonic IV fluids (D5W, 0.45% saline) → free water retention disproportionate to Na+ retention. Modern recommendations favor isotonic IV fluids (LR, NS) for routine postoperative maintenance because of this risk. Recognition: stop hypotonic fluids, switch to isotonic, treat severe symptomatic hyponatremia with hypertonic 3% saline, identify and address ADH triggers (pain control, antiemetic, etc.)
explanations: Correct. Postoperative hyponatremia is a recognized complication driven by two mechanisms: (1) SIADH-like physiology from surgical stress, pain, opioids, nausea, and fasting — all of which promote non-osmotic ADH release; (2) administration of hypotonic intravenous fluids (D5W, 0.45% saline) — adding free water that the patient cannot excrete because of the elevated ADH. The combination produces dilutional hyponatremia in the first 1–3 days postoperatively. Children and women may be particularly susceptible. Modern recommendations (e.g., NICE guidelines): use ISOTONIC IV fluids (LR, NS, balanced salt solutions) for routine postoperative maintenance; avoid hypotonic IV fluids except with specific indications. Management of established postoperative hyponatremia: stop hypotonic fluids; switch to isotonic; correct severely symptomatic with hypertonic 3% saline; identify and address ADH triggers (adequate pain control, antiemetics, treatment of nausea); resolution typically occurs over 2–7 days as the surgical stress resolves.
Incorrect. Pseudohyponatremia features NORMAL plasma osmolality and is unrelated to surgery.
Incorrect. Postoperative hyperglycemia is common but typically mild and would feature high (not low) plasma osmolality.
Incorrect. CSW occurs in CNS surgery (TBI, SAH); not typical hip arthroplasty.
Incorrect. HF could contribute but the temporal pattern with hypotonic fluids points to ADH-driven dilutional hyponatremia.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with chronic SIADH from small cell lung cancer presents with a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Plasma sodium is 112 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate INITIAL treatment for severely symptomatic hyponatremia in this patient?
choices: Hypertonic 3% saline boluses (e.g., 100 mL IV over 10 min, may repeat up to twice if symptoms persist) to acutely raise plasma Na+ by 4–6 mEq/L within the first few hours, addressing cerebral edema and resolving symptoms. Total correction in the first 24 hours limited to ≤8 mEq/L (≤6 in patients at high ODS risk: chronic hyponatremia + alcoholism + malnutrition + hypokalemia). After acute crisis: transition to free water restriction ± tolvaptan; correct underlying cause
explanations: Incorrect. Free water restriction alone is too slow for severe symptomatic hyponatremia (with seizure); hypertonic saline is needed for rapid effect.

Incorrect. Isotonic saline can paradoxically worsen SIADH hyponatremia (the kidney concentrates the saline, retains the water, and excretes the Na+ — net free water gain). Hypertonic saline is needed.

Correct. Severely symptomatic hyponatremia (seizure, coma, severe confusion) requires RAPID partial correction with hypertonic 3% saline to address cerebral edema. Standard regimen: 100 mL of 3% saline IV over 10 minutes, repeated up to twice if symptoms persist. The goal is to raise plasma Na+ by 4–6 mEq/L within the first few hours — enough to resolve cerebral edema and symptoms. Total correction in the first 24 hours is limited to ≤8 mEq/L (≤6 in patients at high ODS risk: chronic + alcoholism + malnutrition + hypokalemia). Once the acute crisis is resolved, transition to free water restriction ± tolvaptan and treat the underlying cause. The trade-off: severely symptomatic patients have ACUTE-on-chronic worsening, where rapid correction is BOTH necessary (to prevent herniation) AND risky (for ODS) — guidelines recommend the partial correction approach.
Incorrect. Mannitol can lower ICP but is not used for hyponatremic seizure (it would worsen the hyperosmolar state).
Incorrect. Loop diuretic alone increases free water excretion modestly but doesn't address the acute cerebral edema.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with chronic SIADH from cancer is being managed long-term. Her plasma sodium has been stable at 124–128 over 6 months and she is asymptomatic. The clinician is choosing initial management. Compared with severely symptomatic acute hyponatremia, which row in the table best matches her appropriate management?

rows: IV hypertonic 3% saline boluses (raise by 4–6 mEq/L over hours)
Hypertonic 3% saline if symptoms; otherwise free water restriction + slow correction
Free water restriction (≤800 mL/day); add tolvaptan if persistent
Mild asymptomatic with adequate solute intake
Address underlying cause; rarely need specific treatment

explanations: Incorrect. Row A describes severe symptomatic acute hyponatremia — appropriate for hypertonic 3% saline boluses but NOT for this patient (chronic and asymptomatic).
Incorrect. Row B describes moderate symptomatic; this patient is asymptomatic.

Correct. Chronic asymptomatic hyponatremia is treated CONSERVATIVELY because rapid correction in chronic hyponatremia carries high risk of osmotic demyelination syndrome. First-line: free water restriction (≤800 mL/day; sometimes ≤500 in severe cases). For SIADH refractory to restriction: tolvaptan (V2 antagonist) — produces selective water diuresis; effective and predictable, but limited by hepatotoxicity (FDA black-box) and need for hospital initiation. Demeclocycline is an older alternative. Treat underlying cause where possible (chemotherapy for SCLC, stop offending drug, etc.). The treatment GOAL is to keep Na+ in a safe range (typically >130) — not necessarily fully normalized; chronic mild hyponatremia is often stable and asymptomatic.
Incorrect. Row D describes mild asymptomatic; this patient has more substantial hyponatremia (124–128) and chronic SIADH from active cancer.
Incorrect. Pseudohyponatremia is a separate category (lab artifact, unrelated to actual sodium homeostasis).

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with chronic SIADH from small cell lung cancer has plasma sodium 124 despite free water restriction to 800 mL/day. The clinician adds tolvaptan. Which of the following best characterizes the mechanism of tolvaptan?
choices: Tolvaptan is a tetracycline antibiotic that inhibits AQP2

Tolvaptan is a SELECTIVE V2-receptor antagonist that blocks ADH binding to V2 receptors on collecting duct principal cells, preventing cAMP-driven AQP2 trafficking. The result is selective free water excretion ('aquaresis') without significant Na+/K+ loss. Useful in chronic SIADH refractory to free water restriction; also approved for ADPKD. Limitations: HEPATOTOXICITY (FDA black-box warning for ADPKD; some hepatotoxicity in SIADH patients, hence treatment limited to 30 days); cost; need for hospital initiation; potential for overly rapid Na+ correction risking ODS — monitor Na+ closely especially in first 24 hours
explanations: Incorrect. ENaC blockade is the amiloride/triamterene mechanism.
Incorrect. NKCC2 inhibition is the loop diuretic mechanism.
Incorrect. Tolvaptan does not affect aldosterone synthesis.
Incorrect. Demeclocycline (a tetracycline) inhibits AQP2 trafficking; tolvaptan is a V2-receptor antagonist.

Correct. Tolvaptan is a competitive antagonist of the V2 vasopressin receptor on collecting duct principal cells. By preventing ADH from activating V2-receptor signaling, it blocks cAMP-driven AQP2 trafficking and prevents free water reabsorption. The result is 'aquaresis' — selective free water diuresis without significant electrolyte loss. Indications: chronic SIADH refractory to free water restriction; advanced ADPKD (slows progression). Limitations: (1) hepatotoxicity — FDA black-box warning in ADPKD use; some hepatotoxicity in SIADH patients; treatment in SIADH limited to 30 days at a time; (2) cost; (3) hospital initiation recommended for first dose due to risk of overly rapid Na+ correction (which could precipitate ODS); (4) close Na+ monitoring in first 24 hours; (5) avoid in significant liver disease. Conivaptan is a non-selective V1a/V2 antagonist used IV for short-term SIADH; not used long-term.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old researcher is studying the pathophysiology of osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS). Which of the following best explains the mechanism by which rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia produces ODS?
choices: In CHRONIC hyponatremia (>48 hours), brain cells lose IDIOGENIC OSMOLES (organic osmolytes — myo-inositol, glutamine, taurine) over 24–48 hours to reduce intracellular osmolality and defend brain volume against the lowered ECF osmolality. Rapid restoration of plasma Na+ shifts water OUT of brain cells faster than the lost osmoles can be replenished (recovery takes days). The intracellular dehydration produces oligodendrocyte injury and demyelination, particularly in the pons (central pontine myelinolysis) and extrapontine sites (basal ganglia, thalamus). Symptoms: dysarthria, dysphagia, paraparesis, locked-in syndrome — often delayed 1–7 days after correction; can be devastating and irreversible
ODS results from direct cellular toxicity of saline
ODS occurs only in acute hyponatremia
ODS is unrelated to correction rate
explanations: Correct. ODS pathophysiology centers on the temporal mismatch between brain volume defense in chronic hyponatremia and the speed of plasma Na+ correction. In CHRONIC hyponatremia, brain cells defend their volume by extruding idiogenic osmoles (organic osmolytes — myo-inositol, glutamine, glutamate, taurine, glycerophosphocholine) over 24–48 hours, reducing intracellular osmolality to match the lowered ECF. This adaptation prevents brain edema and explains why chronic hyponatremia is typically less symptomatic than acute. RAPID correction of plasma Na+ creates a sudden gradient in the OPPOSITE direction — water shifts OUT of brain cells faster than the lost osmoles can be replenished (osmole recovery takes days). The intracellular dehydration injures oligodendrocytes, producing demyelination — particularly in the central pons (central pontine myelinolysis, CPM) and in extrapontine sites (basal ganglia, thalamus, cerebellum). RISK FACTORS: chronic hyponatremia + alcoholism + malnutrition + hypokalemia + severe absolute Na+ depression. Symptoms: dysarthria, dysphagia, paraparesis, quadriparesis, locked-in syndrome, behavioral changes — often DELAYED 1–7 days after correction; can be devastating and partially or completely irreversible. Prevention: limit Na+ correction to ≤8 mEq/L/24h (≤6 in high-risk).
Incorrect. ODS is not direct saline toxicity; it is a secondary consequence of overly rapid water shift OUT of brain cells.
Incorrect. ODS occurs principally in CHRONIC hyponatremia (where idiogenic osmoles have been lost). Acute hyponatremia carries less ODS risk because brain hasn't adapted.
Incorrect. Correction rate is a CRITICAL determinant of ODS risk.
Incorrect. Glucose does not reverse ODS once established.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with chronic alcoholism and Na+ 110 was rapidly corrected to 138 over 8 hours. Three days later he develops dysarthria, dysphagia, and progressive limb weakness leading to a 'locked-in' state. Which of the following best characterizes osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS)?
choices: Headache and visual changes within minutes

DELAYED onset 1–7 days after rapid Na+ correction; symptoms include dysarthria, dysphagia, gaze palsies, paraparesis or quadriparesis, behavioral changes, and 'locked-in' syndrome from pontine demyelination. Extrapontine sites can produce movement disorders (tremor, dystonia). MRI (often delayed by days) shows characteristic central pontine and extrapontine demyelination on T2/FLAIR sequences — the imaging may not appear positive in the first days. Recovery is variable: some recover partially over months; many have permanent deficits. PREVENTION (adhering to correction limits ≤8 mEq/L/24h) is the principal management strategy. RESCUE (if overcorrection occurs): re-administer DDAVP and/or D5W to lower Na+ back into the safe range
explanations: Incorrect. ODS has a DELAYED presentation (1–7 days), not minutes.

Correct. ODS features and timeline: SYMPTOMS APPEAR 1–7 DAYS after rapid Na+ correction (delayed presentation is a hallmark and contributes to misdiagnosis). Pontine signs include dysarthria, dysphagia, gaze palsies, paraparesis or quadriparesis, behavioral changes, and 'locked-in' syndrome (preserved consciousness with paralysis of nearly all voluntary muscles). Extrapontine sites can produce movement disorders (tremor, dystonia, parkinsonism) and altered mental status. MRI (T2 and FLAIR sequences) shows characteristic central pontine demyelination with sparing of corticospinal tracts in the periphery (the classical 'central pons' lesion); extrapontine demyelination can affect basal ganglia, thalamus, internal capsule. CRITICAL: imaging may be NEGATIVE in the first days, only becoming positive 1–2 weeks after symptom onset. Recovery is variable: some recover partially over months; many have permanent deficits. Treatment: supportive care; physical/occupational therapy; some evidence for early reduction of plasma Na+ if overcorrection is recognized. PREVENTION through adherence to correction limits (≤8 mEq/L/24h, ≤6 in high-risk) is the principal management strategy. RESCUE (if overcorrection occurs and ODS has not yet manifested): re-administer DDAVP to limit further water loss, and/or give D5W to lower plasma Na+ back into the safe range — has been shown to reduce ODS risk.
Incorrect. ODS is a CNS disorder, not pulmonary.
Incorrect. ODS is not a renal disorder.
Incorrect. While alcoholism can lead to hepatic encephalopathy, the temporal pattern after rapid Na+ correction points specifically to ODS.

questions.stem: A clinician is comparing acute (<48 hours) and chronic (>48 hours) hyponatremia in two patients. Compared at the same plasma sodium of 120 mEq/L, which row in the table best characterizes the differences?

headers: Risk of ODS during rapid correction
rows: HIGH (water shifts out of brain faster than osmoles can be replenished)
LOW (brain has not adapted, no osmole gradient created during correction)

explanations: Incorrect. Row A describes CHRONIC hyponatremia (lost osmoles, low symptoms, HIGH ODS risk).

Correct. Row B characterizes ACUTE hyponatremia: brain cells have NOT yet lost idiogenic osmoles (preservation persists for ~24–48 hours), so intracellular osmolality is still relatively high; the lower ECF osmolality drives water INTO brain cells, producing CEREBRAL EDEMA → seizures, severe confusion, herniation. CRITICAL CONSEQUENCE: rapid correction of acute hyponatremia carries LOW ODS risk because there are no missing osmoles to be 'overcorrected' — water shifting out of brain cells doesn't leave them dehydrated relative to their baseline. This is why ACUTE severely symptomatic hyponatremia (e.g., exercise-associated hyponatremia in marathoners, postoperative dilutional hyponatremia) can be CORRECTED RAPIDLY with hypertonic saline. CHRONIC hyponatremia, by contrast, has the OPPOSITE profile: preserved brain volume due to lost osmoles, lower symptom burden, but HIGH ODS risk during rapid correction. The clinical management decisions hinge on this distinction.
Incorrect. Lost osmoles + severe symptoms is internally inconsistent; chronic hyponatremia adaptation REDUCES symptoms.
Incorrect. Preserved osmoles + low symptoms is incorrect — acute hyponatremia (preserved osmoles) is symptomatic (cerebral edema).
Incorrect. Acute and chronic differ markedly in physiology and management.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man has plasma sodium 116 mEq/L and weighs 70 kg. The clinician needs to estimate the rate of sodium correction to limit the rise to ≤8 mEq/L over 24 hours. Which of the following best describes the standard approach to calculating sodium correction?
choices: Sodium correction rate is determined empirically without formula
Sodium correction is determined by IV fluid composition only
Sodium correction is independent of patient weight

Estimated change in plasma Na+ from infusion = (infusate Na+ − plasma Na+) / (TBW + 1), where TBW = body weight × 0.6 (men) or 0.5 (women); for a 70-kg man with Na+ 116 receiving 3% saline (Na+ 513): Δ = (513 − 116) / (42 + 1) = 397/43 ≈ 9.2 mEq/L per LITER of infusate. To raise Na+ by 6 mEq/L (the upper safe limit for the first 6–8 hours), give ~650 mL of 3% saline. Calculate target rate to stay within ≤8 mEq/L per 24 hours; monitor frequently
Sodium correction does not require calculation
explanations: Incorrect. Standard practice uses formulas to estimate correction rates, although individual response varies and frequent monitoring is essential.
Incorrect. Both infusate composition AND patient weight enter the calculation.
Incorrect. Patient weight (via TBW) is a key variable.

Correct. The Adrogue-Madias formula (or modifications): Estimated change in plasma Na+ from 1 L of infusate = (infusate Na+ − plasma Na+) / (TBW + 1), where TBW (L) = body weight (kg) × 0.6 for men, 0.5 for women, 0.45 for elderly women. For a 70-kg man with plasma Na+ 116 receiving 3% saline (Na+ 513 mEq/L): TBW ≈ 42 L; ΔNa+ per L = (513 − 116) / (42 + 1) = 397/43 ≈ 9.2 mEq/L per liter. To raise Na+ by 6 mEq/L (upper safe limit for the first 6–8 hours): ~650 mL of 3% saline over the first 6–8 hours. Caveats: (1) the formula assumes pure water gain or loss, ignoring ongoing renal water losses (overestimates correction in DI; underestimates in SIADH); (2) frequent Na+ monitoring (every 2–4 hours) is essential; (3) target is ≤8 mEq/L total in first 24 hours, ≤16 in 48 hours, ≤6/24h in high-risk; (4) if overcorrection occurs, RESCUE with DDAVP and/or D5W is appropriate.
Incorrect. Sodium correction requires calculation and monitoring; ad hoc approaches risk overcorrection.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with chronic hyponatremia (Na+ 118) is being treated with hypertonic 3% saline for severely symptomatic hyponatremia. Within 6 hours his Na+ has risen from 118 to 132 — exceeding the 24-hour limit of 8 mEq/L. He has not yet developed ODS symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
choices: Continue hypertonic saline to fully normalize sodium
Stop all therapy and allow nature to take course

RESCUE FROM OVERCORRECTION: administer DDAVP (desmopressin, 2–4 µg IV) to halt ongoing water loss, AND infuse D5W (electrolyte-free water, e.g., 6 mL/kg over 1–2 hours) to LOWER plasma Na+ back into the safe range. The goal is to bring Na+ back below 8 mEq/L above baseline within 24 hours. Several case series have shown that this maneuver, performed BEFORE ODS develops, reduces or prevents ODS. Further correction is then SLOWED to ≤4–6 mEq/L per subsequent 24-hour periods
explanations: Incorrect. Continuing hypertonic saline would worsen the overcorrection and increase ODS risk.
Incorrect. The patient has overcorrected; ODS prevention requires active intervention.
Incorrect. Dialysis is not the standard rescue approach; D5W + DDAVP are.
Incorrect. Antivirals are unrelated.

Correct. When chronic hyponatremia is overcorrected (>8 mEq/L in 24 hours), the patient is at high risk for ODS. RESCUE: (1) administer DDAVP (desmopressin 2–4 µg IV) to halt ongoing renal water loss and 'lock' the kidney into water-conserving mode; (2) infuse D5W (electrolyte-free water, ~6 mL/kg lean body weight over 1–2 hours, may repeat) to lower plasma Na+ back into the safe range. The goal is to bring Na+ back below 8 mEq/L above baseline within 24 hours. Case series suggest this approach, applied BEFORE ODS develops, reduces or prevents ODS. After rescue, further correction is SLOWED to ≤4–6 mEq/L per subsequent 24-hour periods. Frequent Na+ monitoring (every 2–4 hours) is essential. Some experts recommend prophylactic DDAVP at the START of correction in high-risk patients to limit the rate from the outset.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man with HIV/AIDS has plasma sodium 122 mEq/L. Which of the following is a recognized cause of hyponatremia in HIV-infected patients?
choices: HIV-associated hyponatremia is multifactorial: SIADH from opportunistic CNS infections (cryptococcal meningitis, toxoplasmosis), pulmonary infections (Pneumocystis pneumonia, tuberculosis), or HIV itself; adrenal insufficiency from CMV adrenalitis or direct HIV effects; hypovolemic hyponatremia from chronic GI losses (cryptosporidiosis, mycobacteria); medication-induced (trimethoprim, pentamidine, vincristine); cerebral salt wasting from CNS lesions. Up to 30–60% of hospitalized HIV patients have hyponatremia. Diagnostic workup follows the standard algorithm; treat underlying cause
Hyponatremia in HIV is always pseudohyponatremia
HIV always causes hypernatremia, not hyponatremia
Hyponatremia in HIV is purely psychogenic
explanations: Correct. Hyponatremia is COMMON in HIV/AIDS — up to 30–60% of hospitalized HIV patients. Causes are multifactorial: (1) SIADH from opportunistic CNS infections (cryptococcal meningitis, toxoplasma encephalitis, PML), pulmonary infections (Pneumocystis pneumonia, TB), or HIV itself; (2) adrenal insufficiency — common due to CMV adrenalitis (~50% of AIDS adrenals at autopsy), direct HIV effects, infiltration, or medications (ketoconazole inhibits cortisol synthesis); (3) hypovolemic hyponatremia from chronic GI losses (cryptosporidiosis, mycobacterium avium-intracellulare, isosporiasis); (4) medication-induced — trimethoprim and pentamidine block ENaC (similar to amiloride) producing hyperkalemic acidosis with hyponatremia; vincristine, ifosfamide, and other chemotherapeutics cause SIADH; (5) cerebral salt wasting from CNS infections; (6) hyperlipidemia/protease inhibitor effects can rarely cause pseudohyponatremia. Workup follows the standard algorithm (Posm, volume status, UNa, TSH, cortisol). Treatment depends on the cause: address the opportunistic infection, replace cortisol if adrenal insufficiency, stop offending medications.
Incorrect. HIV is a recognized cause of hyponatremia.
Incorrect. Most hyponatremia in HIV is true hypotonic (SIADH, hypovolemic), not pseudohyponatremia.
Incorrect. HIV is associated with hyponatremia, not hypernatremia.
Incorrect. Hyponatremia in HIV has organic causes.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man develops confusion and seizure after attending a 'rave' where he danced for hours and consumed multiple ecstasy (MDMA) tablets along with copious water. Plasma sodium 118 mEq/L, plasma osmolality 246, urine osmolality 480, urine sodium 65, euvolemic. Which of the following best characterizes MDMA-induced hyponatremia?
choices: MDMA (3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine, 'ecstasy') causes ACUTE hyponatremia via two mechanisms: (1) MDMA stimulates ADH release from the posterior pituitary (SIADH-like physiology), producing inappropriate water retention; (2) MDMA users are warned about hyperthermia and dehydration during prolonged dancing, leading to excessive water intake. The combination — SIADH + excessive water intake — produces dilutional hyponatremia, often acute and severely symptomatic (seizures, cerebral edema, herniation, death). Most cases are women, perhaps because of slightly higher MDMA-induced ADH response. Treatment: hypertonic 3% saline (rapid correction is appropriate because hyponatremia is ACUTE — low ODS risk); discontinue the drug; supportive care
explanations: Incorrect. The plasma osmolality is low; pseudohyponatremia would have normal Posm.

Correct. MDMA-induced hyponatremia is a recognized and sometimes fatal complication of recreational use. Mechanism: (1) MDMA directly stimulates ADH release from the posterior pituitary (via serotonergic and other pathways), producing SIADH-like inappropriate water retention; (2) recreational users are commonly told to 'drink lots of water' to prevent overheating and dehydration during prolonged dancing — the excessive intake combined with impaired water excretion produces dilutional hyponatremia. Most cases are in women (possibly due to slightly different MDMA-induced ADH response). The hyponatremia is ACUTE (developing over hours during the event), so cerebral edema with seizures, coma, and herniation can occur at modest absolute Na+ values. Treatment: hypertonic 3% saline IV bolus for severely symptomatic — RAPID correction is appropriate because the hyponatremia is acute (low ODS risk in acute hyponatremia); supportive care; address hyperthermia and other complications. Several deaths have been reported from MDMA-induced hyponatremic encephalopathy.
Incorrect. Translational hyponatremia features HIGH plasma osmolality.
Incorrect. CSW occurs in CNS disease; MDMA users have intact CNS structurally.
Incorrect. The pattern is euvolemic with concentrated urine and high UNa — SIADH-like, not hypovolemic.
